entries.title: Shopping Is Impossible
entries.summary: It’s never been more exhausting to buy stuff.
entries.content:
For several months, I had been on the hunt for new T-shirts. I vaguely had a vision of what they should look like: not so different from my current T-shirts, except in some way elevated and, more urgent, free of stains or holes. Perhaps they could come in interesting colors? Ideally, they would not be made in sweatshops. There were many, many shirts that seemed to meet these criteria—and with a few clicks, they could be delivered to my doorstep, maybe even by tomorrow. And still, I had purchased none of them.

The problem is the overabundance of options. The problem is too much information, or too little information. The problem is inflation, which has eroded any sense I had of what a T-shirt is supposed to cost. Yet none of them alone can explain why shopping is sucking up more of my time—and maybe yours too. “I don’t think people are actually enjoying the shopping process,” Jaehee Jung, a University of Delaware professor who studies the psychology of fashion, told me. “People spend more time contemplating, and the pre-decision process seems to be taking longer.”

Everywhere, someone is selling something: on Instagram and TikTok, over email and via text. At this point, the boundary between “shopping” and “not shopping” has all but collapsed. There is now a third state: “a little bit shopping.” Shopping is visiting a store or website on purpose, examining the wares, and either buying or not buying them. A little bit shopping is the constant thrum of consumer opportunities that lead mostly to more consumer opportunities. It is looking at a pair of shoes, which leads to looking at another pair of shoes, and another, and then you’re $15 short of the minimum for free shipping and is there anything else you need? It is the feeling of being haunted by the targeted ads that populate your social-media feeds. Even if you never click on them, their very presence contributes to the overwhelming sense that the retail landscape is infinite—so infinite that perfection must exist, and if you look long enough and hard enough, somewhere in the universe, it is probably on sale.

In small doses, a little bit shopping can be fun, a private thrill. It is both a genuine attempt at making a purchase, and a hobby that is infinitely expandable to fill any length of time. Who among us has not scrolled through sweater sales while trapped on a work call? It does not require spending money, nor does it apply to urgent and essential purchases: You don’t a little bit shop for baby Tylenol. “No matter what you’re doing on the computer,” Wendy Woloson, a material historian at Rutgers University at Camden, told me, “it seems like there’s a really easy drift into the shopping mode.”

Unlike brick-and-mortar stores, the internet never closes. You can a little bit shop forever, until you are also a little bit miserable. Shopping in person, then, ought to solve the problem, but it often doesn’t. A survey of 30 retailers by the consulting firm AlixPartners found that, on average, they carried only 9 percent of their online offerings in store. The shoes are out of stock in your size, but have you checked the website? You could stand in line to buy lesser, uglier shoes and be done with it, but why? Online, beautiful shoes are infinite and, in theory, instant.

The more mindful you are about various concerns—overconsumption, worker exploitation, microplastics—the higher the bar climbs: I need not only black pants, but ethical black pants that I can wear to the beach, but also to the opera, and that will be flattering from now until my death. No such pants exist, which is why I don’t have any, but as long as you’re a little bit shopping, the possibility exists.

This state of perpetual shopping has been building for ages. People were a little bit shopping on Amazon and eBay in 2005. But the feeling has become even more acute in recent years as e-commerce has taken over and affiliate marketing has boomed. In addition to sites such as Wirecutter and The Strategist, and every media property with a gift guide, all kinds of influencers have opinions about what you should buy (and may receive a commission if you do).

My own digital social life is a mix of people I know, people I don’t know, brands that post like people, and people launching brands. Here is my high-school lab partner’s baby. Here is a plate of pasta. Here is a picture of an antique lamp for sale from an estate-sale company in Texas. “Everyone is trying to either make money or gain recognition”—and thereby make money—“for their taste,” Isabel Slone, who writes about fashion on the Substack Freak Palace, told me. An influencer can help move $1 million worth of swimsuits in three hours. For a solitary activity, a little bit shopping is perversely social. It is pleasantly intimate, knowing how an opinionated stranger feels about their chef’s knife, or their microwave, or the life-changing sweater that got them through their divorce and is available right now if you click the link in bio. Whether it is helpful consumer education is a separate question: “I do think that the affiliate-link economy,” Slone said, “contributes to this constant feeling of not knowing exactly what is good.”

There is, of course, a way out. You could stop caring. You could embrace the good-enough and the suboptimal, understanding that a little bit shopping is a trap that keeps you shopping all the time. Eventually, I bought a T-shirt, which is in all ways absolutely adequate, and in no sense exceptional. And then, the next day, I saw a post about a T-shirt, which was better. I clicked.

entries.title: What Do Sex and Gender Even Mean Now?
entries.summary: The history of a semantic mess––and a way out of it
entries.content:
In her first argument as a lawyer before the Supreme Court, Ruth Bader Ginsburg famously quoted the abolitionist Sarah Grimké, who said, “I ask no favor for my sex. All I ask of our brethren is that they take their feet off our necks.” At some point, however, Ginsburg was encouraged to use an alternative to the term sex.

“I’m typing all these briefs and articles for you and the word sex, sex, sex is on every page,” her secretary at Columbia Law School told her. “Don’t you know that those nine men”—that era’s Supreme Court justices—“they hear that word, and their first association is not the way you want them to be thinking?” The secretary suggested substituting gender to “ward off distracting associations.”

But sex and gender don’t mean the same thing. The two terms have never been stable. Still, I recall a time when, among educated people, sex was typically understood to refer to matters of biology, such as a person’s reproductive organs, and gender to refer to matters that are socially constructed, such as the norm of dressing little boys in blue pants and little girls in pink dresses. Today, there seems to be no standard usage. Parents throw gender-reveal parties to disclose the sex of their baby. President Trump said in his 2025 inaugural address, “It will henceforth be the official policy of the United States government that there are only two genders: male and female”—but “male” and “female” are sexes. A statute in California defines sex (in part) as follows: “‘Sex’ also includes, but is not limited to, a person’s gender. ‘Gender’ means sex, and includes a person’s gender identity and gender expression.”

The confusion that results from this lost distinction causes problems in academia––see the recent kerfuffle in anthropology––as well as in medicine, law, public policy, and more. People mistake meanings and talk past one another about matters that are fraught even when definitions are clear. How did we get into this semantic mess?

The concept of a “gender role” was introduced in a 1955 paper by the researcher John Money to signify “all those things that a person says or does to disclose himself or herself as having the status of boy or man, girl or woman.” He believed that people born with ambiguous or atypical genitals, whom he called “hermaphrodites or intersexes,” contributed to “this new meaning of gender.” Would such individuals operate in society as men or women? He thought that rearing would better predict a person’s “gender role” than biology.

The term gender identity, first defined as “one’s sense of being a member of a particular sex,” dates back to at least the early 1960s. The psychoanalyst Robert Stoller wrote that “gender role is the overt behavior one displays in society, the role which he plays.” By the ’70s, feminists were the most prominent group to adopt gender and related terms, using them to differentiate biological differences between men and women from differences imposed by society. In the 1972 book Sex, Gender, and Society, the feminist sociologist Ann Oakley suggested that biology may play little or no role in determining gender identity (that is, one’s sense of being a member of a particular sex). If a biological predisposition to a male or female gender identity exists at all, she wrote, it “may be decisively and ineradicably overridden by cultural learning.” In the 1990 book Gender Trouble, Judith Butler challenged the common assumption that gender mirrors sex and is binary, arguing that “a gender cannot be said to follow from a sex in any one way.” Butler also argued that “perhaps this construct called ‘sex’ is as culturally constructed as gender,” and the supposed distinction between them “turns out to be no distinction at all.”

In 1997, the sex researcher Milton Diamond and the psychiatrist Keith Sigmundson reached the conclusion that sex is a distinct and important category. The two revisited a case that Money had included in his research. “The penis of an XY individual was accidentally ablated”—that is to say, severely damaged or removed—“and he was subsequently raised as a female,” the authors recounted. “Initially this individual was described as developing into a normally functioning female.” Money had treated the case as confirmation that nurture reliably overrides nature. But the story later changed: When older, the patient rejected “this sex of rearing” and “switched at puberty to living as a male.” This mattered in part because, the authors explained, “the standard in instances of extensive penile damage to infants is to recommend rearing the male as a female.” They urged doctors to reconsider that practice.

The importance of sex as a category was further affirmed in 2001 by a group of experts convened by the Institute of Medicine (since renamed the National Academy of Medicine). Recounting several public-health guidelines that excluded women of child-bearing age from clinical trials on the erroneous assumption that they “will not differ significantly in response to treatment in most situations,” the report noted: “Sex, that is, being male or female,” is “an important basic human variable that should be considered when designing, analyzing, and reporting findings from studies.”

But the importance of sex as a category of study did not guarantee sex a stable place in scholarship, as the Harvard evolutionary biologist David Haig showed by documenting a dramatic decline in the term sex and a rise in gender in the titles of academic articles between 1945 and 2001. At first, feminist scholarship converged on socially constructed gender and biologically determined sex, Haig wrote, but “that distinction was difficult to maintain,” because “no term remained to refer to situations in which causation was unknown, disputed, or involved an interaction between biology and culture.” Soon gender spread to other disciplines, and eventually gender rather than sex began to appear even in scholarship on the physiology of animals. “Among the reasons that working scientists have given me for choosing gender rather than sex in biological contexts,” Haig wrote, “are desires to signal sympathy with feminist goals, to use a more academic term, or to avoid the connotation of copulation.”

By the 2000s, yet another obstacle to mutual understanding arose: What people meant by gender was changing, not only in academic discourse, but in popular usage. For many of the early feminists, gender was a cage built by society. Parents gave little girls but not little boys Easy-Bake Ovens, reproducing a gendered expectation that girls would grow up to do the cooking. But as the decades wore on, gender came to carry a second meaning, one very different from social norms imposed from the outside. The term now sometimes refers to an internal aspect of a person’s sense of self, or even the essence of who they truly are.

While some people kept using gender as shorthand for something from which they sought liberation––to weaken gender norms was to fight the patriarchy––others saw it as an identity, perhaps innate, that individuals discerned and expressed, and that a just society ought to affirm. In 2014, Facebook announced that users would no longer have to identify as male or female––they could choose among at least 58 “gender” options (including intersex, a term that tells us something about a person’s reproductive or sexual anatomy but not about their gender identity).

That brings us to the present era, when sex and gender loom larger than ever in political, legal, and cultural debates––but usage keeps changing faster than the public can keep up, and many semantic choices are made for reasons other than advancing shared understanding. Three examples help illustrate the dysfunction that can result:

  • When Australia asked individuals to note their sex in its 2021 census, the form gave three options: male, female, and nonbinary, “to allow respondents to participate in the Census when the male and female sex categories did not accurately describe their sex,” the Australian Bureau of Statistics explained. Among the 25,422,788 people that the census counted, 43,220 respondents chose nonbinary.



    But this “did not yield meaningful data,” the bureau later acknowledged, because the respondents hadn’t agreed upon a definition of nonbinary. Among the small number of respondents who selected nonbinary and explained why, “a very small number” indicated that they were intersex; “a small number” noted their sexual orientation; and three-fifths listed a gender identity. The bureau found the data unusable “to estimate the prevalence of any specific group.” The 2026 censuswill ask about sex and gender separately.
  • A 2024 study from JAMA Ophthalmology reviewed pivotal clinical trials in the field between 1995 and 2022. It sought to determine whether sex and gender were used correctly (relying on the National Institutes of Health definitions of sex as “a biological characteristic, reflected genetically by chromosomes and physiologically by sex hormones, internal reproductive organs, and external genitalia” and gender as “an aspect of identity that is self-determined and influenced by sociocultural and environmental factors”). The researchers found that in 85 trials, “over three-quarters applied sex and gender terminology incorrectly” and that “no trial reported how sex or gender were collected,” even though “sex and gender are gaining increasing recognition as important determinants of disease epidemiology, health outcomes, and health care disparities.” The authors concluded that the “policies of biomedical journals on sex and gender are incongruous and uncoordinated” in a way that hurts the field’s mission.
  • In a 2023 interview with Time magazine, the soccer player Megan Rapinoe objected to barring trans women from playing on the same sports teams as biological females. “I see trans women as real women,” she declared. “What you’re saying automatically in the argument—you’re sort of telling on yourself already—is you don’t believe these people are women.” But her formulation elides the fact that women is used variably, sometimes to signify sex and sometimes to signify gender.



    Many proponents of segregating sports by sex do not reject the gender identity of trans women. For example, in the prominent case of Lia Thomas, a trans woman who, controversially, swam on the women’s team at the University of Pennsylvania, 16 teammates sent a letter to Penn that stated, “We fully support Lia Thomas in her decision to affirm her gender identity and to transition from a man to a woman. Lia has every right to live her life authentically. However, we also recognize that when it comes to sports competition, that the biology of sex is a separate issue from someone’s gender identity.” Only by distinguishing between sex and gender can we distinguish between two different viewpoints: that sports leagues should reject a trans person’s account of their own gender, or that gender is irrelevant to this debate and sex alone should govern policy around eligibility to play.

Different ideological groups will continue deploying language that best suits their ends. But we all ought to value terms that are accurate and aid mutual understanding. Clarity is best advanced by using sex to refer to biology––and, when appropriate, to specify whether the particular trait relevant to a given discussion concerns gametes, chromosomes, hormones, anatomy, or some combination. In contrast, gender should be used to refer to matters that are socially constructed––and concepts such as gender norms, gender identity, and gender expression should be used to distinguish different conceptions of gender from one another. If and when disputes arise about whether we’re referring to sex or gender or a mix, speakers should explain why they chose a given term and what precisely they mean by it.

These usage conventions can’t tell us who belongs on what sports team or what is required or forbidden under antidiscrimination law, nor can it settle any number of other debates. But they can help us all better understand and engage in them.

entries.title: The Atlantic Festival announces interview with Colin Kaepernick and exclusive preview of Netflix’s East of Eden, with Florence Pugh, Zoe Kazan, and Bela Bajaria
entries.summary: New speakers include: Senator Mark Kelly, Padma Lakshmi, Joe Kahn, Gina Raimondo, Ben McKenzie, Malcolm Gladwell, Richard Linklater
entries.content:
New speakers include: Senator Mark Kelly, Padma Lakshmi, Joe Kahn, Gina Raimondo, Ben McKenzie, Malcolm Gladwell, Richard Linklater

The Atlantic Festival, back for the second year in New York City from September 17 to 19, is announcing new speakers including the legendary quarterback, philanthropist, and entrepreneur Colin Kaepernick, who will be interviewed by contributing writer Jemele Hill about his forthcoming memoir, The Perilous Fight. The festival will also feature an exclusive first look of Netflix’s limited series East of Eden, a fresh interpretation of John Steinbeck's novel that has been adapted and executive produced by Zoe Kazan, who also serves as co-showrunner. The screening will be followed by a conversation with Kazan, the series’ executive producer and star Florence Pugh, and Bela Bajaria, the chief content officer of Netflix, moderated by staff writer Shirley Li.



These events are part of many new programming announcements today, including: Padma Lakshmi, on the future of creative work and the entertainment industry; Senator Mark Kelly, in conversation with staff writer Mark Leibovich, who recently profiled the senator for the magazine; a discussion about press freedom with Joe Kahn, the executive editor of The New York Times, together with Jeffrey Goldberg, The Atlantic’s editor in chief, and Amna Nawaz, a PBS News Hour co-anchor; former Secretary of Commerce Gina Raimondo, interviewed by the MS NOW anchor Stephanie Ruhle; a conversation with the author, actor, and filmmaker Ben McKenzie; a conversation with the journalist and author Malcolm Gladwell; and a conversation with the filmmaker Richard Linklater.



Also at The Atlantic Festival:

  • Pete Buttigieg; Andrew Card and Karl Rove; Rahm Emanuel; Bumble’s Whitney Wolfe Herd; Representative Chip Roy; Olympian Ibtihaj Muhammad; San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria, Fort Worth Mayor Mattie Parker, and Cincinnati Mayor Aftab Pureval; University of California President James B. Milliken, Mount Holyoke College President Danielle R. Holley, and Columbia University President Jennifer L. Mnookin; State Attorneys General Rob Bonta of California, John Formella of New Hampshire, and David Sunday of Pennsylvania; The Anxious Generation author and Atlantic contributing writer Jonathan Haidt; author and famed Odyssey translator Emily Wilson; The New York Times’ Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan; and live events with Atlantic podcast hosts David Brooks, David Frum, Adam Harris, Hanna Rosin, and Charlie Warzel. The festival involves dozens of The Atlantic’s writers and editors, and today we’ve added Tyler Austin Harper, Honor Jones, Helen Lewis, and Caity Weaver.

Special programming, screenings, and Out and Abouts:



‘A Soundtrack of a Nation’ at Zuccotti Theater (PAC NYC)

Thursday, September 17, 7:30 to 9 p.m. ET

The festival’s opening-night program, “A Soundtrack of a Nation,” a special collaboration with Juilliard, including the composer and pianist Nicholas Britell, the tap dancer and choreographer Michelle Dorrance, the bass-baritone Davóne Tines, and Juilliard President Damian Woetzel; additional performers are to be announced.



Crime and Punishment at Roxy Cinema

Saturday, September 19, 11 to 12 p.m. ET

An exclusive screening of the forthcoming PBS documentary series, which explores the 250-year history of the United States’ criminal legal system, directed by Lynn Novick and executive produced by Ken Burns and Sam Pollard, followed by a discussion with Novick and the poet Reginald Dwayne Betts.



Playing POTUS at Roxy Cinema

Saturday, September 19, 12:30 to 2:30 p.m. ET

A new documentary on presidential parody featuring Saturday Night Live alumni and comedy legends, with director Josh Greenbaum and more speakers to be announced.



Tickets: Single-Day Passes and Out and About tickets are now on sale, along with 2-Day Premier and 2-Day General Admission Passes. Atlantic subscribers receive an exclusive 30 percent discount on festival passes and select Out and About programming.



The 2026 Atlantic Festival is underwritten by Genentech at the Presenting Level; Boston Scientific, Contentful, Edward Jones, and TIAA at the Supporting Level; and Allstate, Calm Health, Ferrero, and Hauser & Wirth and Seabourn Cruise Line at the Contributing Level.



Media and creators interested in covering the festival should reach out to our comms team at [email protected]; in-person seating will be limited and will need to be reserved in advance.



The Atlantic Festival

September 17–19, 2026

Perelman Performing Arts Center and venues around the city, including the Tenement Museum, the Brooklyn Public Library, and Roxy Cinema.

For Passes: theatlantic.com/theatlanticfestival

entries.title: A Deeply Layered Novel About Masculinity
entries.summary: Chang-rae Lee’s new novel examines a young man’s attempt to be tough—and its far-reaching consequences.
entries.content:
Chang-rae Lee’s new novel examines a young man’s attempt to be tough—and its far-reaching consequences.

Tangled themes of violence and masculinity run like buried cables through Chang-rae Lee’s work. One of contemporary American literature’s major chroniclers of manhood, he’s been writing for three decades about assimilation, suburban alienation, and the mystery of how his characters survive loneliness and, often, shocking loss. Lee uses his careful prose to sink slowly and deeply into the minds of men who resist thinking about their feelings, even as they ruminate obsessively about their past griefs.

His new novel, A Tender Age, would belong in this meditative lineage, except that its narrator, a middle-aged man named Jeon-Gi, doesn’t resist emotion in the slightest. He’s as sensitive to—and as fascinated by—its lingering effects as his creator is. And unlike some of Lee’s earlier protagonists, this character wants to know himself. Jeon-Gi opens the book by confessing that he’s consumed by the “nature of certain youthful happenings, how they can become a knot in the flesh that every other occurrence must bypass in order for you to know yourself.” He then recounts, in vivid detail, the events of the summer he turned 11, which have haunted him ever since. The novel wobbles between manhood and boyhood, clarity and confusion, self-knowledge and a windmilling search for identity by a 10-year-old faced with challenges he’s too young to comprehend.

Nearly all of Lee’s fiction—from his debut, Native Speaker (1995), through his war novels, A Gesture Life (1999) and The Surrendered (2010), to his rollicking bildungsroman, My Year Abroad (2021)—shares a worry that the masculine ideals of self-sufficiency, strength, and swagger can lead to brutality. Now, for the first time, Lee traces the concern back to boyhood, a risky move: Young Jeon-Gi’s travails are conventional ones, the fodder of many coming-of-age stories. He gets bullied, lands in trouble defending himself, and then attempts a reinvention. What sets A Tender Age apart is its layered narration, in which a reflective adult and resurrected child together lead the reader onward as Lee strings threats of violence through the text, building thrillerlike tension.

As the eldest child of Korean immigrants, Jeon-Gi feels called on to be “the head of the column” as he, his parents, and his sister navigate life in the United States. Among peers, meanwhile, he feels rising pressure to prove that he’s a cool insider, not a weakling or a “wuss,” to use a word Lee repeats often in the book’s opening section. A lot is at stake in this effort, which abruptly turns Jeon-Gi from a good boy into a troubled youth—a juvenile-justice case, in fact. Lee tracks the adult Jeon-Gi’s fascination with this time in his life, which tested his maturity and masculinity in ways that were both traumatic and exhilarating. In the process, as the novel charts Jeon-Gi’s path toward becoming an American man, Lee dares to linger over the allure of aggression and dominance, probing rather than skirting or accepting it.

Like any coming-of-age story, A Tender Age begins before the Fall. Jeon-Gi, lucky boy, has two Edens: his nuclear family and a “tourniquet tight” gaggle of friends in his neighborhood, a down-at-the-heels 1970s New York suburb where “the adults, for whatever reason, whether they were working a job or not, left us on our own, and to one another.” Jeon-Gi’s mother is an exception. She is the attentive hub of their strikingly close family, and he idolizes her. “I loved my father and my sister to death,” he recalls, “but it was my mother who spun and wove the fabric of my existence.” As her eldest—and as a son—he’s the focus of her doting, which extends to bringing him treats on the otherwise parent-free playground.

Early in the novel, a disturbingly clever bully named Katie Croker targets Jeon-Gi, damaging in one cruel move both his childish dignity and his belief in his mother’s omnipotence. She coerces Jeon-Gi into cursing at his mother, a scene full of the emotional crosscurrents that destabilize and deepen what might seem like a slight book. Deriding his mother’s limited English while clearly envying her warm presence, Katie deploys a well-targeted dig: “You think everybody gets that?” Katie demands of the snack deliveries. “You think it’s normal?”

Jeon-Gi does, in a sense, assume that the treatment he gets is normal, aware though he is that even his sister, Ella, doesn’t receive it. Looking back decades later, he sees that Ella “learned early on to make the best of whatever she got, to always just move on.” Meanwhile, he “expected things to come to me easily, and when they didn’t, I readily gave myself over to the muck of my frustrated thoughts, allowing the foulness to seep in wherever it had a path and then fill my gut with bile.”

After the Katie incident, Jeon-Gi starts to swing between eagerness to delight his parents and impress his friends and a new readiness to indulge a more anti-social side of himself. He’s been initiated into the reality that his playground world, for all of its camaraderie, also harbors dog-eat-dog energy. He starts scamming a boy who’s bad enough at math to need help calculating change for the ice-cream truck: “I liked Paul and Paul liked me,” he recalls, “but because I loved ice cream and because I could, I skimmed him most every time.” “Because I could” is, of course, highly compelling logic when you’re 10; still, Jeon-Gi’s older self sees something more than ordinary childhood behavior in his new urge to exploit.

Jeon-Gi does have good reason for this budding desire for power, as aggression escalates in his unsupervised realm. A former friend, Joshua, begins calling him racist names, and a troubled older boy tails and sadistically harasses him. Fresh from his Katie ordeal, Jeon-Gi decides not to seek parental or peer help. Instead, he devises a private plan that involves bringing his mother’s bread knife to school and that makes him lonelier than he’s ever been in his ten years of life.

Jeon-Gi’s decision to retaliate awakens him to his own capacity and—more important—his own desire to imagine behaving violently. While smuggling the knife into his book bag, he admires the “steely, dead-faced boy” he sees in the mirror and debates whether he wants his truly scary tormentor “scarred for life or simply dead.” Naturally, nothing goes quite as he anticipated, and Jeon-Gi, child that he is, loses control in a conflict with Joshua. In this moment, unlike anywhere else in the text, Lee allows the grown-up Jeon-Gi to dodge his memories. He relates the scene as if he’s blacked it out: “They say I screamed, in Korean and English. You wanna die? Ju-gu-leh? You wanna die right now?” But the lines that come next show that Jeon-Gi has not erased all of the moment. He admits that he can still feel the knife sometimes, and adds, referring to Joshua, “To this day I’ve never seen a person so scared.”

For the rest of the novel, the young Jeon-Gi is consumed by the question of whether he wants to be scary. As he travels through the justice system, the professional verdict is no, he doesn’t. He gets sent to therapy rather than detention, in part because in the world of juvenile courts, as the adult Jeon-Gi recognizes, he’s “a rare creature, akin to some tiny tree primate who foraged only at night, this clean-cut, soft-spoken, somewhat overcourteous Oriental kid who came from an intact and evidently loving, supportive family.” As a child, he hardly grasps the reprieve his demographic rarity offers him. He’s too immersed in the mystery of whether he’s a gentle child or a “dead-faced boy.” Although drawn at times to the latter, he recoils from envisioning his parents burdened with the stigma of a deviant child. As he searches himself for signs of inherent violence, the tenor of the narration wavers between fear and hope, familiar emotional poles in Lee’s work.

The grown Jeon-Gi wavers too. He can hardly bear to remember brandishing the bread knife, yet can’t let go of the thought that he really could have been a violent boy. Lee captures his enthrallment in the novel’s most gripping, surreally disorienting scene—a tour de force in which Jeon-Gi gets sent to visit a prison alongside a group of teenage offenders deemed in need of being scared straight. He clearly doesn’t belong there, and the narrative shifts between wannabe tough guy and nervous child with almost every new paragraph. Even as his adult self recalls hoping for a “tour-ending treat of an ice cream sandwich,” he also remembers feeling thrilled at the “breathtaking” power wielded by a frighteningly charismatic young inmate. By the day’s end, the young Jeon-Gi is newly confident that he can “step outside of a moment in order to commit some transgressive act”—a capacity that most if not all people have, but that he wants to see as a sign of his toughness. When he soon heads to Korean church camp, he is sure that he’s effectively an adult, or at least “someone not easily besieged by emotions.”

Of course, Jeon-Gi is still a child, though in fact his two-week-camp agenda is a mature one in its way: He sets off having decided that he will demonstrate that he’s a good son, not a cause for adult concern. But once he arrives, A Tender Age takes on a threatening tone. Lee weaves in warnings that something awful is coming, and hints that Jeon-Gi will cause it, which freights the boy’s ordinary transgressions—lying about his home life, cheating at games—with suspense. The prose slows down, taking on a luxuriance that makes each scene ominous. When Jeon-Gi and his bunk mates hike to a waterfall, they stand below it in a “natural quarry, its walls composed of a smoother, darker rock almost completely covered in moss.” Beautiful though this “amphitheater of a deep, earthy green that surrounded various pools of water” is, it seems the perfect backdrop for a dangerous spectacle.

Yet A Tender Age’s oscillation between light and dark never lets up. Its foreboding camp scenes are shot through with understated humor and a lingering sense of innocence. Take Jeon-Gi’s infatuation with an independent, enigmatic girl named Susan, which is strikingly pure. The older Jeon-Gi recalls that sex “was as distant from me as the idea of going to a job each day like my father did. I understood it was coming for me but had zero desire.” His crush is all about watchful worship, a fascination with nonconformist autonomy; so is Jeon-Gi’s idolization of his thoughtful counselor, Ben Frost, a religious hippie whom Lee always calls by his full name, as if to remind readers of how snowily white he is.

Counselors aside, the camp is an all–Korean American idyll where for the first time, Jeon-Gi can imagine himself as a hero “at the center of the throng, celebrated by raw throats and hearts.” Still, vengeance and violence reappear when a smooth bully named Dickens becomes his nemesis. Jeon-Gi devises a plan to leave the older boy “marked forever with something like a limp, such that every step he took he’d have to think about what he’d done.”

Ultimately, the camper who goes home “marked forever” is not Dickens but Jeon-Gi. The novel’s climax—about which I will say only that the novel’s escalating tension pays off—bequeaths him the permanent “knot in the flesh” he mentions at the book’s start. In an effort to loosen it, he moves as far as he can from “the old places,” yet, as the novel attests, he remains consumed by this childhood interlude. The identity of the dead-faced boy he saw in the mirror evidently remains the conundrum of his life.

A Tender Age ends without answers, though Lee grants Jeon-Gi one closing moment of clarity, a move he has made in many of his novels. In this case, it’s a memory that is less a knot than a touchstone. He describes a Sunday when, as a “striving, struggling young man,” he broke his rule of avoiding the sites of his childhood and walked by the church that had sent him to camp. As he drew near, “scores of well-dressed congregants and their children were coming out from the nave and down the main steps, like so many fish streaming down the chute of a river.” Church and rushing water—that fraught summer comes to mind, but the image is centrally one of community and connection, of family, of a life of forward momentum. Jeon-Gi can’t join or understand the “swaying, merry-sounding talk” around him: His old congregation has switched languages, from Korean to Chinese. Still, he approaches with great hope. “It could have been wonderful,” he recalls. “I waded in.”
